title: Macular degeneration – Aetiology/Risk factors

title: Macular degeneration – Clinical features
content: Patients present with subacute visual loss, worse centrally, affecting near vision, with gradual loss in dry ARMD and subacute in wet ARMD. Symptoms include difficulty reading, dark adaptation problems, photopsia, glare, and possible Charles-Bonnet visual hallucinations.

title: Conjunctivitis – Definition
content: Allergic conjunctivitis is an inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by an allergic reaction, often occurring alone or in association with hay fever.

title: Conjunctivitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Allergic conjunctivitis may be seasonal, triggered by pollen, or perennial, caused by allergens such as dust mites or washing powder; it is often associated with a history of atopy.

title: Conjunctivitis – Clinical features
content: Allergic conjunctivitis typically presents with bilateral conjunctival erythema and swelling (chemosis), prominent itching, and possible eyelid swelling.

title: Conjunctivitis – Management
content: Management of allergic conjunctivitis includes topical antihistamines and topical mast-cell stabilisers such as sodium cromoglicate and nedocromil to reduce allergic inflammation.

title: Uveitis – Definition
content: Anterior uveitis, also known as iritis, is inflammation of the anterior uvea, specifically the iris and ciliary body.

title: Uveitis – Clinical features: Onset and pain
content: Anterior uveitis typically presents with acute onset ocular discomfort and pain, which may worsen with eye movement or use.

title: Uveitis – Clinical features: Pupil changes
content: The pupil in anterior uveitis may be small and irregular due to sphincter muscle contraction.

title: Uveitis – Clinical features: Photophobia
content: Photophobia is often intense in anterior uveitis, causing discomfort in bright light.

title: Uveitis – Clinical features: Vision changes
content: Blurred vision occurs in anterior uveitis; visual acuity is initially normal but may become impaired as inflammation progresses.

title: Uveitis – Clinical features: Red eye and lacrimation
content: Anterior uveitis presents with a red eye and lacrimation, often accompanied by a ciliary flush, a ring of redness spreading outwards from the cornea.

title: Uveitis – Clinical features: Hypopyon
content: Hypopyon, the presence of pus and inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber, may be seen in anterior uveitis and can produce a visible fluid level.

title: Uveitis – Aetiology/Risk factors: HLA-B27 association
content: Anterior uveitis is associated with the HLA-B27 antigen and may occur in conjunction with other HLA-B27 linked conditions.

title: Uveitis – Associated conditions
content: Anterior uveitis may be associated with ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, Behcet's disease, and sarcoidosis (which may cause bilateral disease).

title: Uveitis – Management: Urgent ophthalmology review
content: Anterior uveitis requires urgent review by an ophthalmologist to prevent complications and initiate appropriate treatment.

title: Uveitis – Management: Cycloplegics
content: Cycloplegic agents such as atropine or cyclopentolate are used in anterior uveitis to dilate the pupil, relieving pain and photophobia.

title: Uveitis – Management: Steroid eye drops
content: Topical steroid eye drops are used to reduce inflammation in anterior uveitis.

title: Blepharitis – Definition
content: Blepharitis is inflammation of the eyelid margins, caused by meibomian gland dysfunction (posterior blepharitis) or seborrhoeic dermatitis/staphylococcal infection (anterior blepharitis).

title: Blepharitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Blepharitis is more common in patients with rosacea and may be caused by meibomian gland dysfunction or seborrhoeic dermatitis and staphylococcal infection.

title: Blepharitis – Pathophysiology
content: Meibomian glands secrete oil to prevent tear film evaporation; dysfunction leads to dry eyes causing irritation and inflammation of eyelid margins in blepharitis.

title: Blepharitis – Clinical features
content: Symptoms are usually bilateral with eyelid margin grittiness, discomfort, redness, sticky eyes in the morning; swollen eyelids in staphylococcal blepharitis; styes, chalazions, and secondary conjunctivitis may occur.

title: Blepharitis – Management
content: Management includes hot compresses twice daily to soften lid margins, mechanical lid hygiene using cotton wool buds with cooled boiled water and baby shampoo or sodium bicarbonate solution, and artificial tears for dry eyes.

title: Infective keratitis – Definition
content: Corneal abrasions are defects of the corneal epithelium, commonly caused by recent local trauma such as fingernails or branches.

title: Infective keratitis – Clinical features
content: Corneal abrasion presents with eye pain, lacrimation, photophobia, foreign body sensation, conjunctival injection, and decreased visual acuity in the affected eye.

title: Infective keratitis – Investigations
content: Fluorescein staining highlights corneal abrasions as yellow-stained areas visible to the naked eye, with enhanced visualization using a cobalt blue filter or Wood's lamp.

title: Infective keratitis – Management
content: Topical antibiotics are recommended for corneal abrasions to prevent secondary bacterial infection.

title: Infective keratitis – Clinical features
content: Corneal foreign body typically presents with eye pain, foreign body sensation, photophobia, watering eye, and red eye.

title: Infective keratitis – Indications for referral to ophthalmology
content: Referral is indicated for suspected penetrating eye injury from high-velocity or sharp objects, significant orbital or peri-ocular trauma, chemical injury after irrigation, organic material foreign bodies, central corneal foreign bodies, or any red flags such as severe pain, abnormal pupils, or reduced visual acuity.

title: Infective keratitis – Risk factors for complications
content: Foreign bodies composed of organic material such as seeds or soil carry a higher risk of infection and complications, necessitating referral to ophthalmology.

title: Infective keratitis – Definition
content: A corneal ulcer is a defect in the cornea, usually caused by an infection. Corneal abrasion refers to corneal defects caused by physical trauma, distinguishing it from infective causes.

title: Infective keratitis – Risk factors
content: Contact lens use is a significant risk factor for infective keratitis. Vitamin A deficiency, especially prevalent in developing countries, also increases susceptibility to corneal ulcers.

title: Infective keratitis – Pathophysiology
content: Infective keratitis can be caused by bacteria, fungi, viruses (herpes simplex and herpes zoster causing dendritic ulcers), and Acanthamoeba, which is linked to contact lens use.

title: Infective keratitis – Clinical features
content: Patients with infective keratitis typically present with eye pain, photophobia, watering of the eye, and focal fluorescein staining of the cornea on examination.

title: Blepharitis – Clinical features of dry eye syndrome
content: Dry eye syndrome presents with dryness, grittiness, or soreness in both eyes, worsening through the day, and watering, especially when exposed to wind.

title: Blepharitis – Clinical features of Meibomian gland dysfunction
content: Symptoms worse on waking, eyelids sticking together on waking, and redness of eyelids suggest dry eye syndrome caused by Meibomian gland dysfunction.

title: Blepharitis – Complications of dry eye syndrome
content: Complications of dry eye syndrome include conjunctivitis or corneal ulceration, indicated by severe pain, photophobia, marked redness, and loss of visual acuity.

title: Blepharitis – Management of dry eye syndrome
content: Eyelid hygiene is the most appropriate management step for dry eye syndrome and helps control blepharitis.

title: Blepharitis – Association with dry eye syndrome
content: Most people with dry eye syndrome have blepharitis, indicating a strong association between the two conditions.

title: Scleritis – Definition
content: Episcleritis is the acute onset of inflammation in the episclera of one or both eyes, often presenting with redness and mild symptoms.

title: Scleritis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Most episcleritis cases are idiopathic; associated systemic conditions include inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis.

title: Scleritis – Clinical features
content: Episcleritis presents with red eye, typically mild pain or irritation (less than scleritis), watering, and mild photophobia; about 50% of cases are bilateral.

title: Scleritis – Clinical features
content: In episcleritis, injected vessels are mobile with gentle pressure on the sclera, unlike scleritis where vessels are deeper and immobile.

title: Scleritis – Investigations
content: Phenylephrine eye drops can differentiate episcleritis from scleritis by blanching conjunctival and episcleral vessels but not scleral vessels; improvement in redness supports episcleritis diagnosis.

title: Scleritis – Management
content: Episcleritis is managed conservatively, often requiring no treatment; artificial tears may be used to relieve symptoms.

title: Benign eyelid disorders – Common types
content: Common benign eyelid disorders include blepharitis (inflammation of eyelid margins causing red eye), stye (infection of eyelid glands), chalazion (Meibomian cyst), entropion (in-turning of eyelids), and ectropion (out-turning of eyelids).

title: Benign eyelid disorders – Blepharitis
content: Blepharitis is inflammation of the eyelid margins that typically leads to a red eye due to irritation and inflammation around the eyelid edges.

title: Benign eyelid disorders – Stye definition
content: A stye is an infection of the glands of the eyelids, commonly caused by staphylococcal bacteria, affecting either the glands of Zeis or Moll externally or the Meibomian glands internally.

title: Benign eyelid disorders – External stye (hordeolum externum)
content: External stye is an infection, usually staphylococcal, of the glands of Zeis (sebum producing) or glands of Moll (sweat glands) located at the eyelid margin.

title: Benign eyelid disorders – Internal stye (hordeolum internum)
content: Internal stye is an infection of the Meibomian glands within the eyelid and may leave a residual chalazion (Meibomian cyst) after resolution.

title: Benign eyelid disorders – Stye management
content: Management of stye includes hot compresses and analgesia; topical antibiotics are recommended only if there is associated conjunctivitis.

title: Benign eyelid disorders – Chalazion definition
content: A chalazion (Meibomian cyst) is a retention cyst of the Meibomian gland presenting as a firm, painless lump in the eyelid.

title: Benign eyelid disorders – Chalazion clinical course
content: Most chalazions resolve spontaneously without treatment, but some cases require surgical drainage if persistent or symptomatic.

title: Benign eyelid disorders – Entropion
content: Entropion is the inward turning of the eyelids, which can cause irritation and damage to the ocular surface.

title: Benign eyelid disorders – Ectropion
content: Ectropion is the outward turning of the eyelids, which can lead to exposure and dryness of the ocular surface.

title: Infective keratitis – Management
content: Management of herpes simplex keratitis requires immediate referral to an ophthalmologist and treatment with topical aciclovir to reduce viral replication and corneal damage.

title: Infective keratitis – Definition
content: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) is the reactivation of varicella-zoster virus in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, causing shingles in the eye area and accounting for about 10% of shingles cases.

title: Infective keratitis – Clinical features
content: HZO presents with a vesicular rash around the eye which may or may not involve the eye itself, and Hutchinson's sign, a rash on the tip or side of the nose indicating nasociliary nerve involvement and increased risk of ocular complications.

title: Infective keratitis – Management
content: Treatment of HZO involves oral antivirals for 7-10 days, ideally started within 72 hours of rash onset; intravenous antivirals may be used in severe or immunocompromised cases; topical antivirals are not used; topical corticosteroids may treat secondary ocular inflammation.

title: Infective keratitis – Complications
content: Ocular complications of HZO include conjunctivitis, keratitis, episcleritis, and anterior uveitis; other complications include ptosis and post-herpetic neuralgia.

title: Infective keratitis – Urgent referral
content: Ocular involvement in herpes zoster ophthalmicus requires urgent ophthalmology review to prevent vision-threatening complications.

title: Diabetic eye disease – Hypertensive retinopathy stage I
content: Stage I hypertensive retinopathy is characterised by arteriolar narrowing and tortuosity, with increased light reflex known as silver wiring.

title: Diabetic eye disease – Hypertensive retinopathy stage II
content: Stage II hypertensive retinopathy is characterised by arteriovenous nipping, where arterioles compress venules at crossing points.

title: Diabetic eye disease – Hypertensive retinopathy stage III
content: Stage III hypertensive retinopathy features cotton-wool spots, flame-shaped and blot haemorrhages, which may collect around the fovea forming a macular star.

title: Diabetic eye disease – Hypertensive retinopathy stage IV
content: Stage IV hypertensive retinopathy is characterised by papilloedema, indicating severe retinal and optic nerve head swelling.

title: Conjunctivitis – Definition
content: Conjunctivitis is the most common eye problem in primary care, characterised by sore, red eyes with a sticky discharge.

title: Conjunctivitis – Bacterial conjunctivitis features
content: Bacterial conjunctivitis presents with purulent discharge and eyes may be stuck together in the morning.

title: Conjunctivitis – Viral conjunctivitis features
content: Viral conjunctivitis presents with serous discharge, recent upper respiratory tract infection, and preauricular lymphadenopathy.

title: Conjunctivitis – Natural history
content: Infective conjunctivitis is normally self-limiting and usually resolves without treatment within 1-2 weeks.

title: Conjunctivitis – Topical antibiotic treatment
content: Topical antibiotics such as chloramphenicol drops (2-3 hourly) or ointment (four times daily) are commonly used to treat bacterial conjunctivitis.

title: Conjunctivitis – Alternative antibiotic for pregnancy
content: Topical fusidic acid is an alternative antibiotic for infective conjunctivitis and should be used twice daily in pregnant women.

title: Conjunctivitis – Contact lens users management
content: Contact lens users with conjunctivitis should have topical fluorescein staining to check for corneal involvement and should not wear lenses during infection.

title: Conjunctivitis – Infection control advice
content: Patients with infective conjunctivitis should be advised not to share towels to prevent spread of infection.

title: Conjunctivitis – School exclusion policy
content: School exclusion is not necessary for children with infective conjunctivitis.

title: Infective keratitis – Definition
content: Keratitis is inflammation of the cornea. Microbial keratitis is a sight-threatening condition that requires urgent evaluation and treatment, unlike conjunctivitis.

title: Infective keratitis – Aetiology Bacterial causes
content: Bacterial keratitis is commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus; Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a frequent cause in contact lens wearers.

title: Infective keratitis – Aetiology Fungal causes
content: Fungal keratitis is a cause of microbial keratitis, often associated with eye exposure to soil or contaminated water.

title: Infective keratitis – Aetiology Amoebic causes
content: Acanthamoebic keratitis accounts for around 5% of cases and is more common with eye exposure to soil or contaminated water; pain is often out of proportion to clinical findings.

title: Infective keratitis – Aetiology Parasitic causes
content: Onchocercal keratitis, also known as 'river blindness', is a parasitic cause of keratitis.

title: Infective keratitis – Aetiology Viral and environmental causes
content: Other causes of keratitis include viral infections such as herpes simplex keratitis and environmental causes like photokeratitis (e.g., welder's arc eye) and exposure keratitis.

title: Infective keratitis – Clinical features
content: Clinical features of infective keratitis include red eye with pain and erythema, photophobia, foreign body or gritty sensation, and sometimes hypopyon.

title: Infective keratitis – Referral criteria
content: Contact lens wearers presenting with a painful red eye require same-day referral to an eye specialist for slit-lamp examination to exclude microbial keratitis.

title: Infective keratitis – Management general
content: Management includes stopping contact lens use until symptoms resolve, topical antibiotics (usually quinolones first-line), and cycloplegics such as cyclopentolate for pain relief.

title: Infective keratitis – Complications
content: Complications of infective keratitis include corneal scarring, corneal perforation, endophthalmitis, and visual loss.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Definition
content: Orbital cellulitis is an infection of fat and muscles posterior to the orbital septum within the orbit, sparing the globe. Periorbital cellulitis is a superficial infection anterior to the septum.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Orbital cellulitis usually results from spreading upper respiratory tract infection from the sinuses. Risk factors include childhood (mean age 7-12), previous sinus infection, lack of Hib vaccination, recent eyelid infection or insect bite, and ear or facial infection.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features
content: Orbital cellulitis presents with redness and swelling around the eye, severe ocular pain, visual disturbance, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia or pain with eye movements, eyelid oedema and ptosis, and sometimes drowsiness or nausea if meningeal involvement occurs.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Differentiation from preseptal cellulitis
content: Reduced visual acuity, proptosis, and ophthalmoplegia or pain with eye movements are features of orbital cellulitis and are not consistent with preseptal cellulitis.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Investigations
content: Investigations include full blood count showing elevated WBC and inflammatory markers, clinical ophthalmological assessment for vision, pupillary defects, proptosis, dysmotility, oedema, erythema, CT with contrast showing orbital inflammation and sinusitis, and blood cultures to identify causative organisms.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Common causative organisms
content: The most common bacterial causes of orbital cellulitis are Streptococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae type B.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Management
content: Orbital cellulitis is a medical emergency requiring hospital admission and urgent senior review, with treatment consisting of intravenous antibiotics.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Definition
content: Preseptal cellulitis, also called periorbital cellulitis, is an infection of soft tissues anterior to the orbital septum, including eyelids, skin, and subcutaneous facial tissue, excluding orbital contents.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Definition
content: Orbital cellulitis is an infection of soft tissues behind the orbital septum and is more serious than preseptal cellulitis.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Infection usually spreads from nearby sites such as breaks in skin, sinusitis, or respiratory tract infections to the tissues surrounding the orbit.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causative organisms include Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, streptococci, and anaerobic bacteria.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Epidemiology
content: Preseptal cellulitis most commonly affects children; 80% are under 10 years old with a median age of 21 months, and incidence is higher in winter due to respiratory infections.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features
content: Patients present with acute onset of red, swollen, painful eye often accompanied by fever.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features
content: Signs include erythema and oedema of eyelids spreading to surrounding skin and partial or complete ptosis due to swelling.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Clinical features
content: Absence of orbital signs such as pain on eye movement, restricted eye movements, proptosis, visual disturbance, chemosis, or relative afferent pupillary defect distinguishes preseptal cellulitis from orbital cellulitis.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Differential diagnosis
content: Important differentials include orbital cellulitis and allergic reactions.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Investigations
content: Blood tests show raised inflammatory markers; swabs of any discharge should be taken; contrast CT orbit helps differentiate preseptal from orbital cellulitis and is indicated if orbital cellulitis is suspected.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Management
content: All cases require referral to secondary care; oral antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav are usually sufficient; children may need admission for observation.

title: Periorbital and orbital cellulitis – Complications
content: Bacterial infection can spread posteriorly into the orbit, causing orbital cellulitis, a more serious condition.

title: Chronic glaucoma – Definition
content: Glaucomas are optic neuropathies associated with raised intraocular pressure (IOP), leading to progressive optic nerve damage and visual field loss.

title: Chronic glaucoma – Pathophysiology
content: In primary open-angle glaucoma, the peripheral iris does not cover the trabecular meshwork, but increased resistance in the trabecular network reduces aqueous humour outflow, causing raised intraocular pressure.

title: Chronic glaucoma – Epidemiology
content: Primary open-angle glaucoma affects less than 1.5% of individuals under 55 years but up to 10% of those over 80 years of age.

title: Chronic glaucoma – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Risk factors for primary open-angle glaucoma include increasing age, Afro-Caribbean ethnicity, family history, myopia, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and corticosteroid use.

title: Chronic glaucoma – Clinical features
content: Primary open-angle glaucoma often presents insidiously with peripheral visual field loss (nasal scotomas progressing to tunnel vision), decreased visual acuity, and optic disc cupping.

content: Ocular manifestations occur in 25% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis, indicating a significant prevalence of eye problems in this population.

title: Scleritis – Definition
content: Scleritis is a full-thickness inflammation of the sclera, usually caused by non-infective processes, leading to a red, painful eye.

title: Scleritis – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Scleritis is commonly associated with autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis (most common), systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

title: Scleritis – Clinical features
content: Scleritis presents with a red eye that may have a violet-bluish hue due to scleral oedema and vessel dilatation; it is classically painful but can sometimes cause only mild discomfort.

title: Scleritis – Clinical features
content: Patients with scleritis commonly experience watering and photophobia, along with a gradual decrease in vision.

title: Scleritis – Management
content: Scleritis requires same-day ophthalmology assessment; first-line treatment is oral NSAIDs, with oral glucocorticoids for severe cases and immunosuppressants for resistant disease or underlying systemic conditions.

title: Retinal detachment – Epidemiology
content: Spontaneous vitreous haemorrhage incidence is around 7 cases per 100,000 patient-years, varying by age and sex according to underlying causes.

title: Retinal detachment – Aetiology/Risk factors
content: Common causes of vitreous haemorrhage include proliferative diabetic retinopathy (>50%), posterior vitreous detachment, and ocular trauma, especially in children and young adults.

title: Retinal detachment – Clinical features
content: Patients present with acute or subacute painless visual loss or haze, red hue in vision, and floaters or shadows/dark spots; visual acuity and field defects vary with haemorrhage severity.

title: Retinal detachment – Investigations
content: Dilated fundoscopy may reveal vitreous cavity haemorrhage; slit-lamp exam shows red blood cells in anterior vitreous; ultrasound rules out retinal tear/detachment if view obscured; fluorescein angiography identifies neovascularisation.

title: Retinal detachment – Investigations
content: Orbital CT is used if open globe injury is suspected in vitreous haemorrhage cases.

title: Retinal detachment – Management
content: Urgent ophthalmology referral is required; manage underlying causes such as optimising diabetes control and laser therapy; consider pars plana vitrectomy if haemorrhage does not clear spontaneously.

title: Retinal detachment – Pathophysiology
content: Bleeding into the vitreous humour arises from disruption of retinal vessels or extension through the retina from other areas, with blood clearing at approximately 1% per day after bleeding stops.
